## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Jarūdapānajātaka* (Ja 256) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens with the verse line *Jarudapānaṁ khaṇamānā* and is framed as an account told by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana concerning merchants from Sāvatthī who set out on a trade journey after making offerings to the Teacher [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, set during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Benares (Vārāṇasī), the Bodhisatta was reborn as a caravan leader (*satthavāhajeṭṭhaka*) directing a trade convoy laden with merchandise [Higham 2004; Fausböll 1879]. Suffering from thirst along their journey, the merchants dug out an old well, discovering jewels and treasure rather than water [Higham 2004; Fausböll 1879]. At the conclusion of the tale (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the principal figures of the past life, revealing that the serpent king (*nāgarājā*) was Sāriputta and the caravan leader was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].
Textual reuse for the *Jarūdapānajātaka* includes extensive overlap with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects matches with the Tibetan translation of the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the tale across four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
